newsitem.title: GERMANY: German taxpayer group sees scant relief in reforms.
newsitem.headline: German taxpayer group sees scant relief in reforms.

text.p: The German government's proposed tax reforms would not go far enough to lighten the taxpayer's burden, a taxpayer group said on Monday.

Even if the reforms go into effect in 1999, as Bonn hopes, average taxpayers will still pay out near-record levels of income in taxes, social security contributions, reunification surcharges and indirect levies, the Taxpayers Association (BdS) said.

Taxes, contributions and other payments in 1997 would consume an average of 45.5 percent of German paychecks, just below the record high of 45.7 percent in 1995 and well above the 1989 level of 41.9 percent, a BdS study revealed.
Bonn's massive tax reform, which was expected to lower tax payments by a net 30 billion marks, would only bring the level down by one to 1.5 percentage points, according to the BdS study.
Without tax reform, the total average burden would rise to 46.2 percent, the group maintained.

"Here it is becoming clear that a net reduction of 20 billion to 30 billion marks as the government wants to institute with tax reform in 1999 is not sufficient by far," BdS president Karl Heinz Daeke said in a statement.
Since unification, taxpayers have had to bear a series of tax and social security increase, as well as the "solidarity surcharge" for rebuilding eastern Germany.
BdS said it recommended a net tax reduction of 80 billion marks offset by priviatising state-owned assets and cutting social and other government programs.
